newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumption slows, bolsters Fed-on-hold view.
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumption slows, bolsters Fed-on-hold view.

text.p: U.S. consumers are spending less.

While that may spell bad news to some retailers, Wall Street pundits said the slowdown might be just enough to keep third quarter Gross Domestic Product growth under 2.5 percent and the Federal Reserve on hold in the near future.

A driving force in the economy, consumer spending currently accounts for two thirds of the nation's GDP and is seen as a key element watched by the Fed when it sets the country's monetary policy, experts said.

"I think the household sector is the key to the economic outlook right now. We've seen sluggish retail activity over the past couple months," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities Inc.

"If it stays sluggish, then we have very good chances of having a tolerable growth rate. But if household spending picks up, we could see continued good growth in the economy and eventual Fed tightening," the economist added.

Recent economic data suggested the consumer sector has been on the weak side in the third quarter as higher long-term interest rates, record debt levels and increasing caution took a toll on spending.
Retail sales, for example, rose a tame 0.2 percent in August against a revised 0.1 percent increase in July. At the time, economists expected sales to be up 0.7 percent.

August consumption rose a brisk 0.6 percent in August but analysts said the data suggested a moderating economy in the third quarter since the rise was seen as a bounceback from low levels in July, when it rose 0.2 percent.
Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc, said the numbers suggest the overall economy might be slowing in the third quarter.
Leahey said he now expects a GDP growth rate between 2.0 and 2.5 percent in the third quarter against a strong 4.7 percent pace in the previous three-month period.
Analysts also said some other factors have contributed to keep a lid on consumer spending, including very restrictive financial conditions.
Long-term interest rates have risen to current levels of 6.85 percent from 6.03 percent in January, when the Fed last cut interest rates.
Also, analysts said a slowdown in bank loan growth, tighter lending standards and a more gradual pace of wealth creation in the equity market are all economic tightening conditions.
"We're constrained by very high levels of debt (on the consumer sector) and also there is not a whole lot of pent-up demand," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
"We've had five and a half years of expansion. People have new cars, they've got new appliances and spending for those big tickets has dropped off," Low added.
Paradoxically, recent income data indicate workers are earning more money. But analysts said caution in spending the extra dough appears to be the word now.
"There still probably is some lingering insecurity, as some Fed officials have alluded, due to technological gains," said Lee Youngdahl, economist at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. Inc.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.5 percent to $11.87 in August against $11.81 in July. In a year-to-year basis, hourly income grew 3.6 percent in August.
Some experts said, however, the current slowdown in spending is just a pause and as soon as consumers catch their breath they will be back into the stores. But no spending boom is predicted.

"We're expecting gains in consumer spending in the fourth quarter, but gains will be coming on the moderate side," Youngdahl said, adding he sees third quarter growth between 2.2 and 2.3 percent. He forecast a 2-3/4 percent GDP growth in the fourth quarter.
